title: He Grew Up Playing Cricket in Rajasthan. On Friday, He Bowled India Out for Ireland.
excerpt: Jai Moondra left Tonk for a master's degree in Dublin, found a cricket club, and five years later walked onto the pitch in Belfast to face the country where it all began — and took a wicket with his very first ball.
body:
When Ireland's left-arm pacer Jai Moondra ran in to bowl his first delivery in international cricket on Friday evening in Belfast, the batter facing him was Sanju Samson — an Indian, like him.

Moondra is from Tonk, a town near Jaipur in Rajasthan. Five years ago, he was finishing his B.Tech at SRM Institute in Chennai and wondering whether to take a corporate job or give cricket one more shot. He chose neither, at least not in the way anyone expected. In 2021, Moondra moved to Ireland to pursue a master's degree in Electronics and Communication Engineering at Technological University Dublin.

He did not leave cricket behind.

## From Leinster to the National Squad

Within weeks of arriving in Dublin, Moondra embedded himself in the local circuit, joining Leinster Cricket Club — one of Ireland's most established sides. His left-arm pace, sharp enough to have once caught the eye of selectors back home but never quite enough to break through, found a different stage.

In Rajasthan, he had played Under-14 cricket alongside Khaleel Ahmed, who went on to represent India. Moondra's own trajectory veered through experimentation — fast bowling, then top-order batting, then left-arm spin, then back to pace — and ultimately through a different continent.

At Leinster, the pieces clicked. Moondra was a key part of the side that won the prestigious Irish Senior Cup in 2023, and his consistent performances in the Inter-Provincial T20 Trophy earned him recognition from Cricket Ireland's selectors. When the squad for the India tour was announced, his name was on it.

## First Ball, First Wicket

The first T20I at the Civil Service Cricket Club, Stormont, was supposed to be straightforward for India. Shreyas Iyer was captaining for the first time, the squad was largely settled, and Ireland had never beaten India in 20 meetings across all formats.

Then Moondra changed the script.

His first delivery in international cricket clattered into Samson's stumps. The 29-year-old from Rajasthan had dismissed one of India's most destructive T20 batters — a man he might have shared nets with in another life — with the very first ball of his career. He finished with figures of 2/25 from his four overs, helping Ireland bowl India out for 148 while chasing 183.

"It was a big stage for me, for my family and my team members. They were all rooting for me, so all I can do is keep calm and keep doing what I have been doing," Moondra told BBC Sport afterward. "Testing myself against India and getting a first-ball wicket — I was trying not to be overwhelmed because we still had nine wickets to go."

He paused, then added: "It is a dream come true to get on to an international platform and play against India. It's something special, a class feeling."

## The Bigger Picture

Moondra was not the only debutant to shine. Matt Hollard, another newcomer, took 3/28, and Matt Humphreys claimed three wickets of his own. Ireland's captain, Lorcan Tucker, led from the front with a half-century that set the platform. It was a team performance, but Moondra's story — the Indian-born fast bowler who dismissed his birth country on debut — was the narrative that landed hardest.

His journey is not unique in its broad strokes. Cricket Ireland has long drawn from a talent pool shaped by migration, and Indian-origin players have featured in Irish domestic cricket for years. But the specifics of Friday's debut — the first ball, the stumps rattled, the country he left behind — gave Moondra's story the texture of something more than a sporting upset.

## The Series Continues

The second and final T20I takes place on Sunday at the same ground. India, trailing 1-0, will be under pressure to avoid a series defeat that would cast an uncomfortable shadow over Iyer's tenure before the England ODIs even begin.

For Moondra, the pressure is different. He has already delivered the moment his family in Tonk had been hoping for — and the moment Ireland's selectors had bet on when they handed a master's student from Rajasthan a cap.

Jai Moondra chose cricket, then chose Ireland. On Friday evening in Belfast, both choices came home.
